lines_note: COMMITTED THIS PASS at 30, and the figure is measured rather than clustered. Every earlier number on this sheet came from the TOTAL column's own ink and moved with the threshold used to group it — 28 in coverage.json 'to the nearest line', 31 at one threshold, 34 at another, and the previous pass could only say '29 to 31, favouring 31'. This pass does not look at the TOTAL column to count rows at all. It fits a line grid to the ENUMERATOR'S OTHER INK — the 22 entries of the three written industry columns, which are read and close against their own printed footings — and asks which line count that ink supports. Thirty does, at an rms of 6.7 px against 19.9, 21.3 and 19.0 for 28, 29 and 31, and 15.4 or worse for every count out to 38. See line_index below and tools/fit_census_line_grid.py, which re-derives all of it from this file's own column_closure block.
no_horizontal_rules: MEASURED ON THIS IMAGE: the sheet carries NO horizontal ruled lines inside the body. A row-darkness profile taken across the empty slaves block finds exactly two strong rules on the leaf — the one under the printed heading and the one above the enumerator's footer — and nothing between them: the largest excess over local background anywhere inside the body is 4.0 grey levels, against 77 to 211 for those two printed rules. The printed form rules this page vertically only. That is the reason a continuation sheet is hard to index, and it is the thing the reading of 33S7-9YYJ-5S could not name when it reported that 'nothing on the image settles which [row] without re-reading the sheet against a row grid anchored on the ruled lines': there is no such grid to anchor on. Every row assignment on these three sheets has to come from the enumerator's own ink, and the only column with an entry on every line is TOTAL.
form_note: The right (continuation) sheet of the 1840 schedule. Columns as printed, left to right: twelve SLAVES columns (six male, six female age bands); TOTAL — number of persons in each family; seven NUMBER OF PERSONS IN EACH FAMILY EMPLOYED IN columns (mining, agriculture, commerce, manufactures and trades, navigation of the ocean, navigation of canals lakes and rivers, learned professions and engineers); PENSIONERS FOR REVOLUTIONARY OR MILITARY SERVICES (ages, names); six DEAF AND DUMB, BLIND, AND INSANE WHITE PERSONS columns; four of the same for coloured persons; and seven SCHOOLS, &c. columns. A blank cell on this form is a zero and is recorded as 0.
closure_note: The enumerator added his own totals at the foot of the sheet. Those printed totals are transcribed under `footer_as_read` and are the committed data on this sheet. Where a per-line reading is attempted it is checked against them and its residual recorded; a reading is never adjusted to make a total come out.

records_note: POPULATED THIS PASS, one record per writing line, 30 of them. It was empty on purpose until now because the line INDEX was the open quantity and 'a record keyed line: 4 would commit an ordinal the sheet does not carry'. line_index closes that, so each record states its line, the y the grid predicts for it, the residual, and what fixes it — a coincident industry entry for 22 of the 30, the grid alone for the other 8. `total` is the family total where it is committed and null where it is not; four lines are null and each says what bounds it. The cells of the twelve slave columns and the seven industry columns are NOT restated per line here: column_closure holds them by column and by y, they close against the enumerator's footings, and re-keying them by line is T-0539's business once the sheet is paired.

footer_total_argument.supersedes: the previous argument, which reached the same answer from a different and weaker place. It rested on 22 numbers summing to 83, on the deposit's mean household size, and on the claim that the footing's middle glyph is the same glyph as the one at y2784 and y2860 — and it named three readings (13 at y647, 11 at y1253, 11 at y2392) whose overturning would let 105 back in.
reasoning: 105 IS NOW REFUTED, NOT DISFAVOURED. Twenty-six of the thirty lines are committed and sum to 126. The four uncommitted lines are families, so each is at least one person, and line 8 carries a commerce 5 and a manufactures 2 and so is at least seven. The column is therefore at least 136. That is 31 over 105, and no reading of the four open lines can close a gap that runs the wrong way.

IT SURVIVES THE ADVERSARIAL RE-READING THE PREVIOUS PASS ASKED FOR. Read the three glyphs it named at their smallest confusable forms — 13 as 3, and both 11s as 4 — and the committed sum falls to 102, for a floor of 112. Still above 105. The refutation does not rest on those three, which is what the previous pass could not say.

165 IS REACHABLE AND IS THE ONLY CANDIDATE LEFT. It asks the four open lines to carry 39 between them, against a floor of 10 and a plausible ceiling near 60 for two two-digit numbers and two families.
footer_total_argument.what_it_now_rests_on: the 26 committed line readings, which are listed one per line in records[] with their evidence, and on the line index that says there are 30 lines and not 28 or 31. Overturning it means overturning the grid or a good half of the column, not three glyphs.

line_index.method: The 22 entry_y values in column_closure (commerce 12, manufactures 9, learned professions 3) are merged where two stand within 30 px — three pairs do, because two industry columns can carry an entry for the same family — and a straight grid y = origin + pitch*n is fitted to what is left, rejecting any fit that puts two anchors on one line and scoring by rms residual. The TOTAL column is not used, which is the whole point: the row index and the numbers are then independent, and a number can be read AGAINST the grid instead of being used to build it.
line_index.jackknife: Refitting with each anchor dropped in turn, 20 of the 22 drops still choose 30 lines. The two that do not are the two END anchors, y658 and y2867: dropping an endpoint shortens the fitted span by a line, so it returns 29 and 28 respectively. No interior anchor carries the result.
